mission: The Ruusan Reformations question -- what the galaxy was told they were for. Before the conversation fully forms, Ben catches Kael in the cargo corridor moving through a private Sith-conscript morning discipline: exact, economical, and unreadable unless you know what surviving a hard institution looks like. Then Ben answers honestly. Sera goes very still. Each survivor grieves the displacement differently. Kael asks about his homeworld; the database returns nothing, and something behind his face changes.
why_now: Before the group can function under pressure, the three have to register what a thousand years has cost them. Ben also has to see Kael as a person before Kael becomes a viewpoint in the coalition -- hence the private morning discipline before the common-area conversation.
conflict: Sera absorbs the Reformations answer in silence. Torin's adaptation is so easy that Ben notices the ease itself. Kael watches the room without entering it -- except Ben has already seen the private ritual that says the distance is discipline, not emptiness. The common area becomes smaller the longer they all sit in it.
turning_point: Kael asks what happened to the Sith world he was taken from. Ben searches and finds nothing — the planet was too small for surviving records. Kael's expression does not change, but the line of his shoulders does.
opening_hook: In the cargo corridor before the others settle, Ben catches Kael moving through a private Sith-conscript morning discipline -- one of those routines whose purpose is invisible until you have lived inside the kind of system that teaches it.
closing_hook: Torin catches Ben's eye across the common area and nods — the nod of a commander acknowledging a subordinate who handled something difficult well. Ben is not sure if he should be reassured or concerned that Torin is already thinking in command structure.
emotional_trajectory: Awkward information exchange -> raw grief (Kael's moment) -> fragile group empathy

stakes.personal: Ben seeing the human cost of what was done to these people
stakes.interpersonal: Building real connection vs. mission-focused alliance
stakes.external: The survivors' displacement is also an intelligence gap — they do not understand the modern galaxy's politics

setting: Aboard the Steady Returns — common area, cramped and intimate
sensory_details: Modern field rations that taste like nothing the survivors remember; the datapad scrolling a galactic history none of them can read fast enough; Kael's silence taking up more of the small space than his body does
action_beats: Ben passes the cargo corridor and catches Kael in a private Sith-conscript morning discipline -- exact, quiet, and over before Ben can decide whether to acknowledge it
Ben pulls up a galactic history archive on the datapad and slides it across the table to Sera
Kael asks about his homeworld and Ben searches the database — the screen returning nothing, the planet too small for surviving records
Torin nods across the common area with a commander's acknowledgment that Ben can't tell is approval or assessment
notes: Kael's approved humanizing beat is the Sith-conscript morning discipline -- private action before explanation, not summary. His homeworld moment remains small and load-bearing -- plants his arc. He is not detached because he does not care; he is detached because caring cost him everything and nobody ever asked. Let the empty database entry do what no line of dialogue could. Diagnostic-voice trap -- Ben should not, in this scene, narrate Kael's psychology or name the defense mechanism. He observes, Desh senses without naming, Torin mediates, Sera absorbs. Kael's cost should land through what the screen does not say. Voice: Allston-brief dialogue, Stover-interior beat permitted only on Ben's recognition of Kael's silence. Prior-EU orientation -- if Mara or Vestara surfaces in the history scroll, each gets one grounding phrase at most, no paragraph.

turning_point_detail.trigger: Kael asks what happened to the Sith world he was taken from, and Ben searches the database.
turning_point_detail.shift: The screen returns nothing—the planet too small for surviving records. Kael's expression does not change, but his shoulders register the cost. Ben sees, for the first time, that Kael's distance is not emptiness but discipline protecting what remains.
turning_point_detail.cost: Ben absorbs the human weight of Veranthos and the thousand-year silence: displacement so complete that even the homeworld is erased from galactic record. The cost also strains the group's cohesion—real connection requires witnessing grief, not managing it.

emotional_arc.start: Awkward information exchange—Ben moving through explanation without feeling its weight.
emotional_arc.shift: Raw grief surfaces when the database returns nothing. Ben's focus tightens on what just changed in Kael's shoulders, the silence taking up more space than his body.
emotional_arc.end: Fragile group empathy—the survivors have registered each other's displacement, and Ben has seen that connection requires more than mission alignment.

key_beats.beat_description: Ben passes the cargo corridor and catches Kael in a private Sith-conscript morning discipline—exact, quiet, economical movement that ends before Ben can decide whether to acknowledge it.
key_beats.state_change: The opening pressure becomes concrete: Ben has seen Kael's invisible survival mechanism before hearing any explanation of displacement.
key_beats.pov_reaction: Ben's instinct pushes toward action rather than explanation—a recognition that some things cannot be named in common areas. His discomfort at witnessing a private ritual registers as a physical tension: the impulse to look away, the choice not to.

key_beats.beat_description: Ben pulls up a galactic history archive on the datapad and slides it across the table to Sera, beginning to answer the Reformations question directly.
key_beats.state_change: The group moves from isolation into shared information. Sera's stillness as she reads becomes the room's new pressure point.
key_beats.pov_reaction: Ben feels the weight of honesty landing—each survivor will process this differently, and he cannot control how. The datapad becomes a physical anchor for a conversation that has no good shape.

key_beats.beat_description: Kael asks what happened to the Sith world he was taken from. Ben searches the database. The screen returns nothing—the planet too small for surviving records.
key_beats.state_change: The scene pivots from abstract displacement to concrete erasure. Kael's homeworld does not exist in the modern galaxy's memory.
key_beats.pov_reaction: Ben's attention narrows to Kael's shoulders—the line of them shifts, a micro-adjustment that registers as the cost landing. Ben does not name what he sees; he feels the silence expand in the small space, and his own breath becomes audible to him.

key_beats.beat_description: Torin nods across the common area—a commander's acknowledgment that Ben cannot read as approval or assessment.
key_beats.state_change: The group's internal structure begins to solidify. Torin is already thinking in command hierarchy, already mediating the survivors' grief through operational framing.
key_beats.pov_reaction: Ben registers the nod as both reassurance and warning. The fragile empathy the group has built is already being threaded through command structure—a pattern that will hold them together and constrain them both.
